query: Consider the following context: High-temperature self-lubricating materials with stable tribological performance across a wide temperature range are essential for advanced mechanical systems under extreme conditions. However, balancing mechanical strength and lubrication efficiency remains a key challenge. In that context, which material can be used for high-performance wide-temperature self-lubricating materials, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A multilayered RHEA coating with an engineered reactive surface layer that forms an in-situ lubricious oxide tribofilm will provide stable self-lubrication over a wide temperature range while preserving high mechanical strength.
generation.material_initial_state: A sputtered nanocrystalline RHEA film (e.g., similar to CuMoTaWV-type alloys) that exhibits high strength but lacks robust self-lubrication at temperatures well above 300 °C.
generation.intervention: Implement a surface/interface engineering strategy by applying a tailored, reactive top layer as part of a multilayered coating design. This layer is optimized to form a lamellar or continuous lubricious oxide film during high-temperature operation.
generation.conditions: Exposure to a wide temperature range from ambient to temperatures significantly above 300 °C under demanding mechanical and thermal loads typical of advanced industrial and aerospace applications.
generation.structural_mediator: The engineered reactive surface layer, which upon oxidation forms a stable lamellar tribofilm that serves as an in-situ solid lubricant.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, the tailored top layer oxidizes in a controlled manner, yielding a lubricious oxide or lamellar tribofilm that minimizes friction and wear. Simultaneously, the underlying RHEA retains its inherent nanocrystalline, high-strength structure, thereby balancing wear resistance with mechanical robustness.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated material is expected to exhibit a significantly lower friction coefficient and reduced wear, along with maintained high strength, over a broad temperature range compared to conventional RHEA coatings without the engineered reactive top layer.
generation.baseline: Standard RHEA films that, while possessing high mechanical strength, do not form stable self-lubricating oxide films across an extended temperature range and thus may suffer increased friction and wear at high temperatures.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis may not hold if the reactive layer consumes too much of the underlying material or if the oxide film formed is unstable or non-uniform at extreme temperatures, potentially compromising the mechanical integrity or lubrication performance.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the controlled kinetics of oxide film formation and its long-term stability across the desired temperature range. Optimization of the layer thickness, composition, and interfacial bonding is required to ensure simultaneous achievement of enhanced lubrication and mechanical robustness.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one with the multilayered RHEA coating incorporating the engineered reactive top layer, and a control set of standard RHEA coatings. Subject both sets to tribological tests across a temperature range from ambient to over 600 °C under identical mechanical loads.
measurements: Wear rate (using profilometry or mass loss measurements)
Mechanical strength retention (using nanoindentation or tensile testing)
Oxide film characterization (using XPS and SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the multilayered coating does not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in friction and wear, and fails to maintain comparable mechanical strength relative to the control sample over the full temperature range, or if the oxide film formed is unstable or non-uniform, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Abstract In the quest of new materials that can withstand severe irradiation and mechanical extremes for advanced applications ( e.g . fission & fusion reactors, space applications, etc.), design, prediction and control of advanced materials beyond current material designs become paramount. Here, through a combined experimental and simulation methodology, we design a nanocrystalline refractory high entropy alloy (RHEA) system. Compositions assessed under extreme environments and in situ electron-microscopy reveal both high thermal stability and radiation resistance. We observe grain refinement under heavy ion irradiation and resistance to dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation in the form of low defect generation and evolution, as well as no detectable grain growth. The experimental and modeling results—showing a good agreement—can be applied to design and rapidly assess other alloys subjected to extreme environmental conditions. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Power stations

Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical engineering

decision.trend: Only the fourth paper (PMC7304825) explicitly addresses tribological behavior in a high-entropy alloy (CuMoTaWV) film. The progression there was to deposit a nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy by sputtering, then anneal to improve adhesion. This gave good hardness, strong wear resistance, and stable friction at room temperature and 300 °C. However, it did not demonstrate self-lubrication across a truly wide temperature range. Achieving long-range lubrication stability at higher temperatures while maintaining mechanical strength remains a gap.
decision.unsolved: Ensuring a reliable self-lubricating mechanism from near-ambient to high temperatures (far beyond 300 °C) without compromising the underlying alloy’s mechanical strength is not yet resolved by the documented approaches.
decision.lever: Design a multilayered RHEA-based coating with an in-situ formed lubricating oxide or lamellar tribofilm to reduce friction from ambient to elevated temperatures. Control the thickness and morphology of the built-in solid lubricant layer to optimize both wear resistance and mechanical performance under extreme conditions.
decision.why: Building on the sputtered RHEA film approach, adding a tailored top layer or interphase that develops a lubricious oxide film in operation is a logical extension to achieve stable lubrication while retaining high mechanical strength across a broader temperature range.
